discovery: Invention of the insulated-gate bipolar transistor (IGBT) and the physics of power semiconductor devices
motivation: Around 1980 at General Electric, B. Jayant Baliga invented the insulated-gate bipolar transistor. It combines MOS gate control with bipolar conductivity modulation in a single silicon device. The physical insight was that injecting minority carriers into a lightly doped drift region could greatly lower on-resistance while keeping voltage-controlled switching. The IGBT now controls power in motor drives, trains, electric vehicles, solar and wind inverters and household appliances. The energy it has saved over the decades is enormous, with a corresponding cut in CO2 emissions. Baliga also set out the 'Baliga figure of merit', which ties breakdown field, mobility and bandgap to power-device performance. It predicted the advantage of wide-bandgap semiconductors such as SiC and GaN, which are now in industrial use. This is device physics that began with careful understanding of carrier transport in semiconductors and ended in technology that benefits everyone. It fully deserves the Nobel Prize.
